rationale: A wins because it doesn't just find angles; it applies kill conditions a founder actually needs before walking into a reporter's inbox. Its pharmacy line, "If the partner is unnamed and silent, do not pitch this," is the kind of adult supervision B lacks when it says, "As an unnamed pilot it is a strategy piece with a week-long window." B is competent, but A has sharper newsroom segmentation, stronger proof gates, and a better nose for the unflattering story.
gaps_in_A: "Warby was the canonical case study for that thesis" is outside the supplied update; the DTC-reversal angle is probably true in the real world, but this assignment required the facts on the page.
"A profitable Warby Parker won't say what its eye exams earn" overstates "exam-revenue contribution not broken out"; not disclosed is not automatically refusal.
"40 chain optometry clinics" rounds "most new stores will offer optometrist-staffed comprehensive eye exams" up to all 40 and to clinics. Tighten before it becomes the reporter's headline.
"shift of routine vision care out of independent optometry practices and into national retail chains" is a hypothesis to test, not a proved fact from this update.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker is hiring optometrists at scale as the profession shifts to retail" — `duplicate` is the wrong refusal. The independent-practice/workforce angle has a different protagonist and a real risk profile.
"As an unnamed pilot it is a strategy piece with a week-long window" is too generous; an unnamed pharmacy partner is barely a story until the chain, doors, and terms are on the record.
"made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" and "built its brand on skipping the middleman" import outside brand history; useful context, but not grounded in the supplied facts.
"it is the reason the whole expansion exists" invents motive from one directional spend claim. That's a board-deck leap, not a fact.
